## The question

[Question about a specific graph theorem](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5103561/question-about-a-specific-graph-theorem), asked by [Honer_300](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1668701/honer-300) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2025-10-23; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I have been told to prove the theorem that a graph $G$ has an independent set of size at least $k$ containing vertex $v$ iff $G-N(v)$, where $N(v)$ is the set of vertices containing $v$ and all of its neighbors, contains an independent set of at least size $k-1$. The way the question is structured assumes it to be true, but I feel I have found a counterexample.
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
> I feel that if you were looking for an independent set of size 5, and did the check on vertex $a$, the size check would pass, but $a$ would not be part of the independent set. Am I missing something?
>
>   [q-1]: mL1zW6ID.png
:::

In your example, $G-N(a)$ removes $a$ and $b$. This has an independent set of size 4, namely $\{g,h,i,j\}$. And $\{a,g,h,i,j\}$ is an independent set of size 5.
